deep.reconstruction:
Context: Euler models wall friction on a moving fluid element MNmn as dry friction proportional to the normal pressure on the wall (§§8-9). The pressure is expressed as a head p, the wetted perimeter is u and the element length is ds. The friction force is λ p u ds. The mass is zz·ds, where zz is the cross-sectional area. So the frictional retardation (deceleration, in head-type units) is λ p u / zz. The geometry therefore enters only through the ratio perimeter/area, which is the reciprocal of what later hydraulics calls the hydraulic radius (hydraulic mean depth).

On this page (§11), for a circular section of area zz, Euler sets n = z/√π. This is consistent with zz = π n², so n is the radius. The retardation 2λp/n then becomes 2λp√π/z. He absorbs the constant 2√π into one empirical coefficient α = 2λ√π, writing the retardation as α p / z, with λ = α/(2√π). He remarks that for experiments with circular pipes only α needs to be known.

§12 is methodological. To get the friction one must know the wall pressure p everywhere. But p depends on the velocity, and the velocity is reduced by friction, so it is unknown. Hence one must proceed in the analysts' manner: treat the unknowns as known, set up the balance equations, and solve them simultaneously, i.e. a self-consistent differential formulation.

§13 sets up the canonical problem (Tab. VI, Fig. 2). A reservoir AB is kept permanently full (infinite width or continuous supply). It drains through a pipe or channel ABMNCD of arbitrary, variable shape and cross-section, discharging at orifice CD.

§14 states that after an initial acceleration the flow quickly becomes steady. The next page then takes the steady state and asks how much friction reduces the efflux velocity below the Torricelli value √(DE). This leads to a one-dimensional energy/momentum balance along the pipe axis with a pressure-dependent loss term.
errors: On the previous page (§10) Euler says the circular section has 'diametrum = n' but uses u = 2πn and zz = πnn, which hold for radius n. This page continues the same convention (n = z/√π gives zz = πn²), so 'diameter' should read 'radius' (semidiameter). The formulas themselves are internally consistent. If n really were the diameter, the retardation would be 4λp/n, not 2λp/n.

The physical premise, that fluid wall friction is proportional to the pressure on the wall (like Coulomb/Amontons solid friction), is wrong. Pipe-flow losses depend essentially on velocity (roughly velocity squared for turbulent flow, linear for laminar flow) and not on the static pressure level. This is a known limitation of Euler's frictional hydraulics, not a slip of calculation.

ideas.what: Frictional retardation proportional to wetted perimeter divided by cross-sectional area (u/zz). For a circle this gives a coefficient times p over the radius, folded into a single empirical constant α
ideas.modern_name: hydraulic radius / hydraulic mean depth (A/P) as the geometric parameter of wall resistance
ideas.where_published: E260 itself (Novi Comment. Acad. Sci. Petrop. 6, 1756/57, publ. 1761); unsure whether Truesdell's Opera omnia II.12/II.13 introductions single this out

ideas.what: Absorbing geometric constants into one experimentally determined coefficient α for circular pipes
ideas.modern_name: empirical friction coefficient (cf. Chézy C, Darcy f)

ideas.what: Methodological remark: pressure, velocity and friction are mutually dependent, so treat the unknowns as known and solve the coupled equations (analytic method)
ideas.where_published: common in Euler's hydraulics papers (e.g. E258-E260 series)

ideas.what: Setup of steady efflux from a constant-head reservoir through a pipe of arbitrary variable shape, with the frictional reduction of the Torricelli velocity
ideas.modern_name: one-dimensional steady pipe flow with head loss (extended Bernoulli equation)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Daniel Bernoulli / Euler; head-loss form to Weisbach, Darcy
ideas.where_published: E260; Euler's hydraulic machine papers of the 1750s

missed.claim: Euler isolates perimeter/area (the inverse hydraulic radius) as the sole geometric factor of wall friction per unit mass, for arbitrary section shapes. He gives rectangle, square and circle cases on the previous page. This predates Chézy's use of A/P, though it is attached to a pressure-proportional rather than velocity-dependent friction law. It may be under-credited in hydraulics histories, but Truesdell probably notes Euler's frictional hydraulics, so its novelty is modest.
missed.quote: retardationem a frictione oriundam exprimere quaeamus per αp/z
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: This is a historical-priority nuance for the hydraulic radius concept. It has no modern technical significance.

deep.surprise_reason: The page is routine algebra plus problem set-up. The only point of interest is the early appearance of the perimeter/area (hydraulic radius) factor, and that is embedded in a physically incorrect friction law and is probably known to historians of hydraulics.
transcription_corrections: 'coguoſci' should read 'cognoſci'. This is a printing error visible in the scan, not a machine-transcription error.
Marginal note 'Tab VI. Fig. 2.' belongs beside the start of §13 ('...nicae principiis repetam... Sit igitur vas'), not after §13.
